scenario.title: Protecting Information
scenario.description: This lab walks through a cybersecurity protection scenario on a 3D interactive stage that you can orbit and zoom. Offense: an Outsider checks digital information, access controls, backups, computer protection, network detection, vulnerabilities, incident response, and recovery systems to identify weaknesses without changing or stealing anything. Defense: the security team encrypts records, removes unnecessary access, creates backups, activates antivirus and IDS protection, fixes weaknesses, prepares an incident response plan, tests recovery, and checks all security procedures. First, use the toolbox on the left to build the scene yourself — one object at a time. Then work through the simulated terminal to play out each step.

scenario.title: CIA Triad Scenario

Offense: an Outsider checks whether medical reports are private, accurate, and available by reviewing file protection, report verification, change history, backup services, storage, and emergency recovery. Defense: the security team protects private reports, verifies report accuracy, records file changes, restores backup services, manages storage, creates emergency backups, tests recovery, and performs a final CIA Triad check. First, use the toolbox on the left to build the scene yourself — one object at a time. Then work through the simulated terminal to play out each step.

scenario.title: Social Engineering Scenario
scenario.description: This lab walks through a Social Engineering scenario on a 3D interactive stage that you can orbit and zoom. Offense: an Outsider identifies an employee, builds trust, creates urgency, and uses pretexting and manipulation to obtain restricted access through impersonation. Defense: the security team detects the behavior, verifies identity, blocks the contact, restricts access, and trains employees to recognize manipulation, pretexting, urgency, and impersonation. First, use the toolbox on the left to build the scene yourself — one object at a time. Then work through the simulated terminal to play out each step.
offenseAlgorithm: Step 1: Identify target → execute find-users --dept=HR → use the result to advance the attack.
Step 2: Study behavior → execute view-patterns --user=employee → use the result to advance the attack.
Step 3: Build trust → execute start-contact --role=vendor → use the result to advance the attack.
Step 4: Create urgency → execute send-alert --priority=urgent → use the result to advance the attack.

Step 3: Stop interaction → execute block-contact --source=unknown → use the result to block, contain, remove, restore, or strengthen the target.
Step 4: Restrict access → execute deny-request --source=unverified → use the result to block, contain, remove, restore, or strengthen the target.

Defense: the security team scans attachments, blocks and quarantines the malicious file, removes the malware, patches the weakness, and confirms the systems are clean. First, use the toolbox on the left to build the scene yourself — one object at a time. Then work through the simulated terminal to play out each step.
offenseAlgorithm: Step 1: Create malicious file → execute create-malware --type=generic → use the result to advance the attack.
Step 2: Attach to email → execute attach-file --target=email → use the result to advance the attack.
Step 3: Send phishing email → execute send-email --target=employee → use the result to advance the attack.
Step 4: Wait for download → execute wait-for-download --target=attachment → use the result to advance the attack.
Step 5: Run malware → execute execute-malware --target=employee-computer → use the result to advance the attack.
Step 6: Check infection → execute check-infection-status --target=computer → use the result to advance the attack.
Step 7: Spread to network → execute spread-malware --target=network → use the result to advance the attack.
Step 8: Review damage → execute show-impact --type=malware → use the result to advance the attack.
defenseAlgorithm: Step 1: Scan email attachments → execute scan-attachment --target=email → use the result to block, contain, remove, restore, or strengthen the target.
Step 2: Block malicious file → execute block-file --type=malicious → use the result to block, contain, remove, restore, or strengthen the target.
Step 3: Run antivirus scan → execute run-antivirus-scan --target=computer → use the result to block, contain, remove, restore, or strengthen the target.
Step 4: Quarantine infected file → execute quarantine-file --target=malware → use the result to block, contain, remove, restore, or strengthen the target.
Step 5: Remove malware → execute remove-malware --type=generic → use the result to block, contain, remove, restore, or strengthen the target.
Step 6: Patch vulnerability → execute apply-patch --target=computer → use the result to block, contain, remove, restore, or strengthen the target.
Step 7: Monitor network → execute monitor-network --type=malware-activity → use the result to block, contain, remove, restore, or strengthen the target.
Step 8: Confirm system clean → execute verify-system --type=final → use the result to block, contain, remove, restore, or strengthen the target.

scenario.title: Trojan Scenario
scenario.description: This lab walks through a Trojan scenario on a 3D interactive stage that you can orbit and zoom. Offense: an Outsider disguises malware as free useful software, tricks an employee into installing it, hides the malicious process, and opens a backdoor for remote access. Defense: the security team scans downloads, blocks untrusted installs, detects the hidden process, closes the backdoor, removes the trojan, and confirms the system is clean. First, use the toolbox on the left to build the scene yourself — one object at a time. Then work through the simulated terminal to play out each step.
offenseAlgorithm: Step 1: Create fake software → execute create-trojan --disguise=free-tool → use the result to advance the attack.
Step 2: Upload to website → execute upload-file --target=download-site → use the result to advance the attack.
Step 3: Trick employee to download → execute lure-download --target=employee → use the result to advance the attack.
Step 4: Employee installs program → execute install-program --target=employee-computer → use the result to advance the attack.
Step 5: Hide malicious process → execute hide-process --name=trojan → use the result to advance the attack.
Step 6: Open backdoor → execute open-backdoor --target=computer → use the result to advance the attack.
Step 7: Gain remote access → execute connect-remote --target=employee-computer → use the result to advance the attack.
Step 8: Review access gained → execute check-access --target=computer → use the result to advance the attack.
defenseAlgorithm: Step 1: Scan downloaded file → execute scan-file --target=download → use the result to block, contain, remove, restore, or strengthen the target.
Step 2: Detect fake software → execute check-software-source --target=download → use the result to block, contain, remove, restore, or strengthen the target.
Step 3: Block untrusted install → execute block-install --source=untrusted → use the result to block, contain, remove, restore, or strengthen the target.
Step 4: Detect hidden process → execute scan-processes --type=hidden → use the result to block, contain, remove, restore, or strengthen the target.
Step 5: Close backdoor → execute close-backdoor --target=computer → use the result to block, contain, remove, restore, or strengthen the target.
Step 6: Remove trojan → execute remove-malware --type=trojan → use the result to block, contain, remove, restore, or strengthen the target.
Step 7: Update firewall rules → execute update-firewall --type=block-unknown → use the result to block, contain, remove, restore, or strengthen the target.
Step 8: Verify system clean → execute verify-system --type=final → use the result to block, contain, remove, restore, or strengthen the target.

scenario.title: Worm Scenario
scenario.description: This lab walks through a Worm scenario on a 3D interactive stage that you can orbit and zoom. Offense: an Outsider releases a self-spreading program that finds a network weakness and copies itself from computer to computer without any employee action. Defense: the security team detects the unusual traffic, isolates infected computers, patches the network weakness, removes the worm, and confirms the network is back to normal. First, use the toolbox on the left to build the scene yourself — one object at a time. Then work through the simulated terminal to play out each step.
offenseAlgorithm: Step 1: Create self-spreading program → execute create-worm --type=self-spreading → use the result to advance the attack.
Step 2: Find network weakness → execute scan-vulnerabilities --target=network → use the result to advance the attack.
Step 3: Release worm → execute release-worm --target=network → use the result to advance the attack.
Step 4: Infect first computer → execute infect-host --target=computer-1 → use the result to advance the attack.
Step 5: Spread automatically → execute auto-spread --target=connected-devices → use the result to advance the attack.
Step 6: Infect more computers → execute infect-host --target=computer-2 → use the result to advance the attack.
Step 7: Slow down network → execute overload-network --type=traffic → use the result to advance the attack.
Step 8: Review spread → execute show-impact --type=worm-spread → use the result to advance the attack.
defenseAlgorithm: Step 1: Detect unusual traffic → execute monitor-network --type=unusual-traffic → use the result to block, contain, remove, restore, or strengthen the target.
Step 2: Isolate infected computers → execute isolate-hosts --type=infected → use the result to block, contain, remove, restore, or strengthen the target.
Step 3: Block spreading path → execute block-connection --type=worm-path → use the result to block, contain, remove, restore, or strengthen the target.
Step 4: Patch network weakness → execute apply-patch --target=network → use the result to block, contain, remove, restore, or strengthen the target.
Step 5: Scan for worm → execute scan-network --type=worm → use the result to block, contain, remove, restore, or strengthen the target.
Step 6: Remove worm → execute remove-malware --type=worm → use the result to block, contain, remove, restore, or strengthen the target.
Step 7: Restore normal traffic → execute restore-network --type=normal → use the result to block, contain, remove, restore, or strengthen the target.
Step 8: Confirm network clean → execute verify-system --type=final → use the result to block, contain, remove, restore, or strengthen the target.

steps.activity log: Worm auto-spread in progress
steps.dashboard: The worm is spreading to connected devices.

steps.activity log: Second computer infected
steps.dashboard: Computer 2 is infected.

steps.activity log: Network traffic overloaded
steps.dashboard: Network performance is degraded.

steps.activity log: Worm spread displayed
steps.dashboard: The worm has spread across multiple computers.

steps.activity log: Unusual traffic scan completed & Infected computers isolated & Security Analyst secured
steps.dashboard: Unusual spreading traffic was detected. Infected computers are ISOLATED.

steps.command info: Blocks the network path the worm used so it cannot continue moving between devices. Then, fixes the network weakness the worm used so the same entry point cannot be used again.
steps.activity log: Worm spreading path blocked & Network weakness patched & Network Administrator secured
steps.dashboard: The spreading path is BLOCKED. The network weakness is FIXED.

steps.activity log: Network-wide worm scan completed
steps.dashboard: All infected computers were identified.

steps.command info: Removes the worm from every infected computer so the infection is fully cleared.
steps.activity log: Worm removed from all hosts
steps.dashboard: The worm is REMOVED.

options.A: It spreads by itself without needing a person to click anything
options.C: It requires a password to run

mcqs.q: What did the worm use to move between computers?

options.A: A weakness in the network

mcqs.q: What should defenders do first when a worm is spreading?

options.A: Isolate infected computers from the network

mcqs.q: Why is patching the network weakness important after removing a worm?

options.A: So the same weakness cannot be used again
options.B: So the worm can spread faster

mcqs.q: What effect can a spreading worm have on network performance?

options.A: It can slow the network down
options.B: It always speeds up the network
options.C: It has no effect on traffic

scenario.description: This lab walks through a Ransomware scenario on a 3D interactive stage that you can orbit and zoom. Offense: an Outsider delivers ransomware, encrypts an employee's files, locks the file server, and demands payment to unlock them. Defense: the security team isolates the infected computer, stops the encryption, removes the ransomware, restores files from backup, and confirms recovery. First, use the toolbox on the left to build the scene yourself — one object at a time. Then work through the simulated terminal to play out each step.
offenseAlgorithm: Step 1: Deliver ransomware → execute deliver-payload --type=ransomware → use the result to advance the attack.
Step 2: Run on computer → execute execute-file --target=employee-computer → use the result to advance the attack.
Step 3: Encrypt files → execute encrypt-files --target=employee-files → use the result to advance the attack.
Step 4: Lock file server → execute lock-files --target=file-server → use the result to advance the attack.
Step 5: Show ransom note → execute display-message --type=ransom-demand → use the result to advance the attack.
Step 6: Demand payment → execute request-payment --amount=high → use the result to advance the attack.
Step 7: Threaten deletion → execute send-threat --type=deadline → use the result to advance the attack.
Step 8: Review impact → execute show-impact --type=ransomware → use the result to advance the attack.
defenseAlgorithm: Step 1: Isolate infected computer → execute isolate-hosts --type=infected → use the result to block, contain, remove, restore, or strengthen the target.
Step 2: Stop file encryption → execute stop-process --target=ransomware → use the result to block, contain, remove, restore, or strengthen the target.
Step 3: Remove ransomware → execute remove-malware --type=ransomware → use the result to block, contain, remove, restore, or strengthen the target.
Step 4: Restore from backup → execute restore-backup --target=employee-files → use the result to block, contain, remove, restore, or strengthen the target.
Step 5: Check backup integrity → execute verify-backup --target=file-server → use the result to block, contain, remove, restore, or strengthen the target.
Step 6: Report incident → execute report-incident --type=ransomware → use the result to block, contain, remove, restore, or strengthen the target.
Step 7: Patch entry point → execute apply-patch --target=computer → use the result to block, contain, remove, restore, or strengthen the target.
Step 8: Confirm recovery → execute verify-system --type=final → use the result to block, contain, remove, restore, or strengthen the target.

scenario.title: Man-in-the-Middle Scenario
scenario.description: This lab walks through a Man-in-the-Middle scenario on a 3D interactive stage that you can orbit and zoom. Offense: an Outsider sets up a fake Wi-Fi network, intercepts an employee's traffic on public Wi-Fi, and captures login information as it travels to a website. Defense: the security team detects the fake network, warns the employee, turns on a VPN and encryption, checks website certificates, and resets any exposed credentials. First, use the toolbox on the left to build the scene yourself — one object at a time. Then work through the simulated terminal to play out each step.
offenseAlgorithm: Step 1: Set up fake Wi-Fi → execute create-fake-network --name=free-wifi → use the result to advance the attack.
Step 2: Wait for connection → execute wait-for-connection --target=employee-laptop → use the result to advance the attack.
Step 3: Intercept traffic → execute intercept-traffic --target=network → use the result to advance the attack.
Step 4: Capture login data → execute capture-data --type=login-credentials → use the result to advance the attack.
Step 5: Read unencrypted data → execute read-traffic --type=plaintext → use the result to advance the attack.
Step 6: Alter data in transit → execute modify-data --target=session → use the result to advance the attack.
Step 7: Impersonate website → execute spoof-website --target=login-portal → use the result to advance the attack.
Step 8: Review stolen data → execute show-impact --type=mitm → use the result to advance the attack.
defenseAlgorithm: Step 1: Detect fake network → execute scan-networks --type=suspicious → use the result to block, contain, remove, restore, or strengthen the target.
Step 2: Warn employee → execute send-alert --type=unsafe-network → use the result to block, contain, remove, restore, or strengthen the target.
Step 3: Turn on VPN → execute enable-vpn --target=employee-laptop → use the result to block, contain, remove, restore, or strengthen the target.
Step 4: Check website certificate → execute verify-certificate --target=login-portal → use the result to block, contain, remove, restore, or strengthen the target.
Step 5: Encrypt connection → execute enable-encryption --type=connection → use the result to block, contain, remove, restore, or strengthen the target.
Step 6: Block suspicious network → execute block-network --type=fake-wifi → use the result to block, contain, remove, restore, or strengthen the target.
Step 7: Reset compromised credentials → execute reset-credentials --target=employee → use the result to block, contain, remove, restore, or strengthen the target.
Step 8: Confirm secure connection → execute verify-connection --type=final → use the result to block, contain, remove, restore, or strengthen the target.

scenario.title: Zero-day Exploit Scenario
scenario.description: This lab walks through a Zero-day Exploit scenario on a 3D interactive stage that you can orbit and zoom. Offense: an Outsider finds a previously unknown software weakness, tests it, and uses it to gain access before a fix exists. Defense: the security team detects unusual activity, isolates the affected computer, reports the weakness to the vendor, applies a temporary fix, and installs the official patch once released. First, use the toolbox on the left to build the scene yourself — one object at a time. Then work through the simulated terminal to play out each step.
offenseAlgorithm: Step 1: Search for unknown weakness → execute search-vulnerability --type=unknown → use the result to advance the attack.
Step 2: Test the weakness → execute test-exploit --target=software → use the result to advance the attack.
Step 3: Confirm weakness works → execute confirm-exploit --target=software → use the result to advance the attack.
Step 4: Attack the software → execute run-exploit --target=employee-computer → use the result to advance the attack.
Step 5: Gain access → execute gain-access --target=computer → use the result to advance the attack.
Step 6: Avoid detection → execute evade-detection --method=unknown-signature → use the result to advance the attack.
Step 7: Explore the system → execute explore-system --target=computer → use the result to advance the attack.
Step 8: Review impact → execute show-impact --type=zero-day → use the result to advance the attack.
defenseAlgorithm: Step 1: Detect unusual activity → execute monitor-network --type=unusual-behavior → use the result to block, contain, remove, restore, or strengthen the target.
Step 2: Isolate affected computer → execute isolate-hosts --type=affected → use the result to block, contain, remove, restore, or strengthen the target.
Step 3: Report to vendor → execute report-vulnerability --target=vendor → use the result to block, contain, remove, restore, or strengthen the target.
Step 4: Apply temporary fix → execute apply-workaround --target=software → use the result to block, contain, remove, restore, or strengthen the target.
Step 5: Wait for official patch → execute check-patch-status --target=vendor → use the result to block, contain, remove, restore, or strengthen the target.
Step 6: Install patch → execute install-patch --target=software → use the result to block, contain, remove, restore, or strengthen the target.
Step 7: Scan for reinfection → execute scan-system --type=post-patch → use the result to block, contain, remove, restore, or strengthen the target.
Step 8: Confirm system secure → execute verify-system --type=final → use the result to block, contain, remove, restore, or strengthen the target.

mcqs.q: What is a zero-day exploit?

options.A: An attack that uses a software weakness before it is publicly known or fixed

mcqs.q: Why is a zero-day attack hard to stop with normal tools?

options.A: The weakness is unknown, so there is no existing fix or detection rule for it
options.C: It requires a password to work

mcqs.q: What should be done after finding unusual activity from an unknown cause?

options.A: Isolate the affected computer
options.B: Ignore it since the cause is unknown
options.D: Wait a few weeks before responding

mcqs.q: Why should a newly found weakness be reported to the software vendor?

options.A: So the vendor can create an official fix
options.B: So the exploit can be sold
options.D: So the computer stays isolated forever

mcqs.q: What should be done once the vendor releases an official patch?

options.A: Install the patch to close the weakness for good
